title: Stellantis CEO says Wayve tie-up can cut self-driving costs, development time
source_used: Reuters story as carried by Investing.com (read via TradingPedia and BigGo), cross-checked with The Next Web's own report from the Turin event
key_facts: Stellantis chief executive Antonio Filosa spoke on Friday 9 Oct 2026 at the Wave technology event in Turin alongside Wayve chief executive Alex Kendall.
Filosa said the Wayve collaboration is meant to shorten development cycles and lower the cost of advanced driver-assistance systems.
The partnership targets level 2++ assistance, which allows hands-off driving while the driver must still supervise.
Filosa said Stellantis's current development timeline is around 24 months and that automotive scale is a complementary asset that will help decrease costs.
The partnership, announced in May, puts Wayve's AI driving software into Stellantis's STLA AutoDrive platform; the first launch is targeted for North America in 2028.
The companies showed hands-free driving in development versions of the Fiat 500e and Maserati Grecale, extending a demonstration first shown on a Jeep Grand Cherokee earlier this year.
Wayve also works with Nissan and Mercedes-Benz, and says its technology is meant to work across brands.
Kendall said at the event that Wayve wants systems running on less than $1,000 of hardware (The Next Web).
quote_evidence: Speaking alongside Wayve CEO Alex Kendall at the Wave technology event in Turin, Filosa emphasized that large-scale deployment will be critical to reducing the cost of hands-free driving and accelerating consumer uptake.

Filosa noted that a major advantage of collaborating with specialist technology providers is the potential to shrink Stellantis’ current development timeline, which he said stands at around 24 months.
During the Turin event, Stellantis and Wayve showcased hands-free driving capabilities in development versions of the Fiat 500e and Maserati Grecale.
why_it_matters_hint: A large carmaker is buying in AI driving software to bring hands-off driver assistance to ordinary cars sooner and cheaper, with a first launch targeted for 2028.
